issues.legal_issue: A registered sale deed is presumed validly executed unless the person challenging it rebuts that presumption with reliable evidence.
material_facts: The disputed property was conveyed by a registered sale deed that recited the consideration and the vendor’s voluntary execution of it.
The person who prepared and witnessed the deed testified that the vendor executed it on his instructions and of his own free will; the trial court found this evidence credible.

The challenger relied on a doctor’s evidence and a medical certificate, but the doctor had prepared the certificate from memory and the trial court did not find the evidence sufficient to show that the vendor could not understand the deed.
The trial court found the deed valid, but the first appellate court and the High Court held it invalid and placed the burden of proving its validity on the purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court and the High Court erred in holding the registered sale deed invalid and in placing the burden of proof on the purchaser; the challenger did not rebut the presumption of valid execution.
issues.legal_principle: A registered document carries a presumption of valid execution, and the burden of rebutting it lies on the person challenging the transaction. The Court relied on Prem Singh v. Birbal (2006) 5 SCC 353 and Vishwanath Bapurao Sabale v. Shalinibai Nagappa Sabale (2009) 12 SCC 101.

rule.if: civil_property_dispute and registered_sale_deed and execution_supported_by_credible_evidence and challenger_lacks_reliable_rebuttal

predicates.civil_property_dispute: The parties litigate rights in property through a civil proceeding.
predicates.registered_sale_deed: The disputed transfer is recorded in a registered sale deed.
predicates.execution_supported_by_credible_evidence: Evidence from a person involved in preparing or witnessing the deed supports that the transferor executed it voluntarily.
predicates.challenger_lacks_reliable_rebuttal: The person challenging the deed does not produce reliable evidence sufficient to rebut valid execution.

issues.definition: When a property dispute concerns a registered sale deed and credible evidence supports its execution without a reliable rebuttal, the deed stands.

issues.legal_issue: A claimed oral gift under Mohammedan law is not established unless the required elements of the gift, including delivery of possession, are proved.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that his father had orally gifted him a house occupied by tenants.
The claimant did not show how possession was delivered to him, that he collected rent, paid property-related taxes, or took steps to have the property recorded in his name.
The alleged will said to accompany the oral gift was found fabricated by the trial court.
The purchaser, by contrast, produced evidence of possession and acts of ownership, including proceedings against tenants and a change in municipal records.
issues.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish the essential requirements of the oral gift, particularly delivery of possession, and the lower courts erred in accepting the gift claim.
issues.legal_principle: A valid oral gift under Mohammedan law requires the donor’s intention to gift, the donee’s acceptance, and the donee’s taking possession; constructive possession may suffice in appropriate circumstances. The Court relied on Abdul Rahim v. Sk. Abdul Zabar (2009) 6 SCC 160.

predicates.property_claim_based_on_mohammedan_oral_: A claimant bases a claim to property on an oral gift said to have been made under Mohammedan law.
predicates.not_possession_delivered_or_constructive: The claimant does not establish that possession was delivered, directly or constructively, to the donee.

issues.definition: A claim based on a Mohammedan oral gift fails when the claimant does not establish delivery of possession to the donee.

issues.legal_issue: The party alleging undue influence must plead and prove circumstances showing that the other party could dominate the transferor’s will and used that position to obtain an unfair advantage.
material_facts: The claimant challenged the mortgage and sale documents on grounds including undue influence, mental infirmity, and an alleged relationship between the purchaser and the transferor.
The pleadings concerning undue influence were vague, and the claimant did not prove that the purchaser could dominate the transferor’s will or used such a position to obtain an unfair advantage.
The transferor executed the mortgage and sale documents during his lifetime and did not challenge them.
The evidence relied on to establish mental infirmity was not sufficient to show that the transferor lacked capacity when executing the sale deed.
issues.conclusion: The claimant failed to prove undue influence or fraud, and the documents were not shown to be vitiated on those grounds.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 16(1) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, undue influence requires a relationship enabling one party to dominate the will of another and the use of that position to obtain an unfair advantage. The Court relied on Subhas Chandra Das Mushib v. Ganga Prasad Das Mushib, AIR 1967 SC 878, which applied the stages explained in Raghunath Prasad v. Sarju Prasad, AIR 1924 PC 60.

predicates.transaction_challenged_for_undue_influen: A party to a civil dispute alleges that a transaction was procured by undue influence.
predicates.not_dominating_position_proved: The challenger does not prove that the other party was in a position to dominate the transferor’s will.
predicates.not_unfair_advantage_proved: The challenger does not prove that the other party used such a position to obtain an unfair advantage.

issues.definition: An undue-influence claim fails when the challenger does not prove either a position to dominate the transferor’s will or the use of that position to obtain an unfair advantage.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgagor’s right of redemption may be extinguished as against a mortgagee when that mortgagee purchases the mortgaged property and thereby acquires the equity of redemption.
material_facts: The property had been mortgaged to two mortgagees, one of whom later purchased the property from the mortgagor under a sale deed.
The claimant sought redemption as alternative relief in a suit whose principal relief challenged the mortgage and sale documents.
The High Court treated the suit as a simple redemption action and ordered payment of the mortgage amount and delivery of possession.
issues.conclusion: The sale to the mortgagee was an act of the parties by which the right of redemption was extinguished as against that purchaser; the High Court was not right to decree redemption in the manner it did.
issues.legal_principle: Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 recognizes the right of redemption, subject to its proviso permitting extinction by an act of the parties or a court decree. The Court relied on Shivdev Singh v. Sucha Singh (2000) 4 SCC 326 concerning the statutory nature of the right of redemption and explained that the later purchase of the property by a mortgagee merged that mortgagee’s mortgage interest with the purchase.

predicates.mortgage_redemption_dispute: A party seeks to redeem property subject to a mortgage.
predicates.mortgagee_purchases_mortgaged_property_f: A mortgagee later purchases the mortgaged property from the mortgagor.

issues.definition: A claim to redeem against a mortgagee fails when that mortgagee has purchased the mortgaged property from the mortgagor.

issues.legal_issue: A court granting redemption of a mortgage must follow the prescribed procedure for preliminary and final decrees in a redemption suit.
material_facts: The High Court ordered payment of the mortgage amount and delivery of possession as a simple redemption decree.
It did not follow the procedure for a preliminary and final decree prescribed for redemption suits.
Redemption was sought only as alternative relief in a suit principally seeking declarations that the mortgage and sale documents were void.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s redemption decree and direction for delivery of possession could not be sustained because the required procedure was not followed.
issues.legal_principle: Order 34 Rules 7 and 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 prescribe the procedure for preliminary and final decrees in a mortgage-redemption suit. Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 governs the right of redemption.

predicates.court_grants_mortgage_redemption: A court grants relief requiring redemption of mortgaged property.
predicates.prescribed_preliminary_and_final_decree_: The court does not follow the required procedure for making preliminary and final decrees in a redemption suit.

issues.definition: A redemption decree is unsustainable when a court grants redemption without following the required preliminary- and final-decree procedure.

issues.legal_issue: A suit to obtain a declaration concerning an instrument or to cancel or set it aside must be brought within the applicable three-year limitation period running from accrual of the right to sue or knowledge of the relevant facts.
material_facts: The suit sought declarations that the mortgage and sale documents were void and sought cancellation of the sale deed.
The claimant admitted that he learned of the sale deed shortly after his father’s death.
The suit was filed more than three years after that knowledge and after the dates on which the claimant pleaded that the cause of action arose.
issues.conclusion: The suit challenging the validity of the mortgage and sale documents was barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 58 and 59 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 prescribe a three-year limitation period for the relevant declaratory and cancellation claims, running respectively from when the right to sue accrues and when the facts entitling the plaintiff to seek cancellation or setting aside first become known.

predicates.suit_seeks_declaration_or_cancellation_o: A civil suit seeks a declaration concerning an instrument or seeks to cancel or set it aside.
predicates.plaintiff_knew_relevant_facts: The plaintiff knew the facts that entitled the plaintiff to bring the relevant claim.
predicates.more_than_three_years_elapsed_before_fil: More than three years passed after the applicable starting point before the suit was filed.

issues.definition: A claim for a declaration concerning or cancellation of an instrument is time-barred when the plaintiff knew the relevant facts and filed more than three years after the applicable starting point.

issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court that reverses or varies a trial court’s findings must address the points for determination and evidence and give reasoned findings supporting its decision.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the suit after assessing the documentary and oral evidence and finding the mortgage and sale deed valid.

The first appellate court reversed the trial court, including by making findings about the transferor’s need for the transaction and the adequacy of consideration without supporting pleadings and evidence.
The first appellate court did not answer all points arising for determination or adequately explain its departure from the trial court’s findings.
The High Court proceeded on the footing that the case was a simple mortgage-redemption suit and did not adequately determine the factual and legal issues concerning the documents.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court did not properly discharge its duty to give reasoned findings, and the High Court’s judgment could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 requires an appellate judgment to state the points for determination, decisions, reasons, and relief. A first appeal is a valuable right involving rehearing on fact and law, and a court reversing trial findings must show conscious consideration of the evidence and reasons for differing. The Court relied on Vinod Kumar v. Gangadhar (2015) 1 SCC 391, B.V. Nagesh v. H.V. Sreenivasa Murthy (2010) 13 SCC 530, Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari (2001) 3 SCC 179, and Madhukar v. Sangram (2001) 4 SCC 756.

predicates.first_appeal_from_trial_decree: A party pursues a first appeal from a trial court’s decree.
predicates.appellate_court_reverses_trial_findings: The appellate court reverses or varies findings made by the trial court.
predicates.appellate_court_fails_to_address_evidenc: The appellate court does not address the relevant evidence and points for determination or explain its departure from the trial court’s findings.

issues.definition: A judgment reversing trial findings is unsustainable when the appellate court fails to address the relevant evidence and give reasons for its decision.
